sections.title: How many people came through the gate?

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The first band is about to play at the county fair. The supervisor calls from the south gate. She wants to know whether to open another entrance. Meanwhile, the treasurer wants yesterday’s attendance figure for a meeting tomorrow. The same scanners can help both people. Which of them needs an answer while people are still walking through the gate?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: The supervisor. A count that arrives tomorrow gives her no chance to move today’s queue. I’d feed incoming admissions into a running calculation. For the treasurer, I could collect yesterday’s records as a set, check them, and issue a daily total.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: That gives us stream processing and batch processing. The stream keeps taking new events. A batch has a boundary, such as all records selected for one day. You can keep the original events and use both approaches. Now let’s listen to exactly one five-minute interval. It starts at eleven fifty-five and ends just before noon.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: I’ll run the counter. The first admission, Robin, reaches me on time. The second, Wren, also reaches me on time. The scanner didn’t hear the acknowledgment for Wren, so it sends that message again with the same event identifier. Those bird names stand for individual scans in our example.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: It’s noon. Pause here and say two numbers aloud. How many messages reached you? How many distinct admissions do you know about?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Three messages. Two admissions. Robin counts once and Wren counts once. If I counted deliveries, the retry would look like another person. I’d keep the scan identifier with the record so I can recognize the repeat.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: A third scanner was briefly offline. At one minute past noon it delivers Lark, a new scan. Lark happened one minute before noon. For this report, we group by the time people crossed the gate, and our procedure accepts this delay. Which interval gets the extra admission?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: The earlier interval. Lark’s event time is eleven fifty-nine. Its arrival time is twelve oh one. At noon I could tell the supervisor we had seen two distinct admissions. Once Lark arrives, I can revise that figure to three and preserve when I made the correction.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Change one detail. The technician wants to measure the load on the receiver and counts every incoming message in the minute it arrives. Pause and explain where Lark goes now, and whether Wren’s retry matters.

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: Lark goes into the minute starting at twelve oh one. And yes, Wren’s retry matters to the receiver because it had to handle the message again. I'd label one chart admissions by scan time and the other messages by arrival time. Two different answers can both be right when readers know what the counter measures.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: One last call from the gate. A ticket holder leaves and is later admitted again. Staff give the second admission a fresh scan identifier. Our measure is admissions, including reentry. Would keeping only one record per ticket work?

turns.speaker: learner
turns.text: That would erase a genuine admission. Keep one record per admission event. If the treasurer asks for unique ticket holders instead, that is a different calculation. Before I publish either figure I want a sentence that says what counts once, which clock sets the interval, and how we handle a delayed record.

turns.speaker: learner
